note: Authored Study Room quiz items for C. Code items (fix_bug, write_snippet) are validated by execution: every reference solution passes its tests in the sandbox runner, every buggy snippet fails them, and every short_answer and mcq_code program was compiled with -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -fsanitize=undefined and its output compared with the stated answer.

items.prompt: A function must add the integers 1 through n inclusive. Which loop header visits exactly those values?
choices: for (long long i = 1; i < n; i++)
for (long long i = 1; i <= n; i++)
for (long long i = 0; i < n; i++)
for (long long i = 1; i <= n + 1; i++)
items.explanation: Starting at 1 and testing i <= n visits 1, 2, ..., n. i < n stops one value early, starting at 0 and testing i < n visits 0 through n - 1, and i <= n + 1 visits n + 1 as well.

items.prompt: Inside a function you write `long long total;` with no initializer and then run `total += x;` in a loop. What is the status of the first `+=`?
choices: total starts at 0 because C zero-fills local variables
total keeps the value it had at the end of the previous call to the function
It reads an indeterminate value, which is a bug
The compiler refuses to compile a variable that has no initial value
items.explanation: Automatic (local, non-static) variables are not initialized: they hold an indeterminate value until you assign one, and reading it is a bug. Only static-duration variables start at zero. Write `long long total = 0;`.

items.prompt: What does this program print?
items.explanation: i takes the values 10, 6 and 2; the next value, -2, fails the condition i > 0. The body runs three times.

items.prompt: Type exactly what this program prints.
items.explanation: continue skips the rest of the body for even i, so only 1, 3 and 5 are added: 1 + 3 + 5 = 9.

items.prompt: Type exactly what this program prints (spacing is ignored).
items.explanation: The condition i-- > 0 compares the old value with 0 and then decrements, so the body sees 2, 1, 0 and the loop ends when i was 0. This is the safe way to count down with an unsigned type, which can never be negative; `i >= 0` would be always true.

items.prompt: In your own words: what is an accumulator in a loop, what must you decide before the first iteration, and what does it hold after each iteration?
items.answer: An accumulator is a variable that carries the result for everything the loop has visited so far. It must be declared outside the loop and given an explicit initial value before the first iteration (for a sum, 0, because C does not initialize local variables), and after each iteration it holds the result for all the elements processed up to that point, which is the invariant that explains why the final value is correct.

items.prompt: This function should return the sum of the even integers from 2 through n inclusive (0 when n is below 2), but it gives wrong answers for some inputs. Fix it.
items.explanation: With i < n the loop never visits n itself, so an even n is left out. The condition must be i <= n.

items.prompt: Write count_multiples(n, k): return how many integers from 1 through n are divisible by k. n is between 0 and 1000 and k is between 1 and 1000.
items.explanation: Visit every integer from 1 through n, test divisibility with the remainder operator, and count the matches in an accumulator that starts at 0.

items.prompt: A caller has `long long x = 5;` and calls `bump(x);`, where `void bump(long long v) { v = v + 1; }`. What is the value of x after the call?
choices: 6, because v is another name for x
5, because v is a copy of x
Indeterminate, because bump returns no value
The program does not compile, because a parameter cannot be assigned
items.explanation: C passes arguments by value. v is a local copy initialized from x, so changing v leaves x untouched. To change the caller's variable the function must receive its address (a pointer).

items.prompt: A function declared `long long sign(long long v)` returns 1 when v > 0 and -1 when v < 0, but has no statement for v == 0, so control can reach the closing brace. What happens when it is called with 0 and the caller uses the result?
choices: It returns 0 automatically
It returns the last value that was computed in the function
The program is rejected at link time
The behaviour is undefined
items.explanation: Using the value of a non-void call whose function ended without a return statement is undefined behaviour in C. Compilers diagnose the missing path with -Wreturn-type (the exercise runner turns it into an error). Make every path return a value.

items.prompt: What does this program print?
items.explanation: The argument add(1, 2) is evaluated first and gives 3. twice(3) calls add(3, 3), which returns 6.

items.prompt: Type exactly what this program prints.
items.explanation: v is a copy of a: it becomes 11 inside the function, but a stays 1 in the caller. p holds the address of b, so *p += v updates the caller's variable: b becomes 1 + 11 = 12.

items.prompt: Type exactly what this program prints.
items.explanation: Integer division in C truncates toward zero: 7 / 2 is 3 and -7 / 2 is -3 (not -4).

items.prompt: A function must give its caller two results, for example a quotient and a remainder. Because C passes arguments by value, how can it do this? Describe at least one approach.
items.answer: A function can return only one value directly. It can return one result with return and write the other through a pointer parameter that the caller passes in (an output parameter), because the pointer is a copy of an address and writing through it changes the caller's variable. Alternatively it can return a struct that holds both values, or take two pointers and return a status code.

items.prompt: clamp(value, low, high) should return low when value < low, high when value > high, and value otherwise (low <= high). It returns wrong results for values outside the range. Fix it.
items.explanation: The two out-of-range branches return the opposite bound. A value below low is replaced by low, and a value above high by high.

items.prompt: Write a small helper function min2(a, b) that returns the smaller of two long long values, and use it to write min_of_three(a, b, c), which returns the smallest of three values. Both functions must be in your answer.
items.explanation: A helper defined before its use keeps each function to one purpose; min_of_three is the helper applied twice.

items.prompt: Which fragment grows the heap array `arr` to `new_cap` elements without losing the old block when realloc fails?
choices: arr = realloc(arr, new_cap * sizeof *arr);

realloc(arr, new_cap * sizeof *arr);
/* keep using arr */

int* tmp = realloc(arr, new_cap * sizeof *arr);
if (tmp != NULL) { arr = tmp; }
items.explanation: On failure realloc returns NULL and leaves the original block allocated. Assigning the result straight to arr overwrites the only pointer to that block and leaks it. A temporary lets you keep arr valid and report the failure. Ignoring the return value discards the possibly moved block.

items.prompt: Which of these calls has defined behaviour?
choices: free(p) a second time, after p was already freed
free(&local) where local is an automatic variable
free(p + 1) where p came from malloc(10)
free(NULL)
items.explanation: free(NULL) does nothing. Freeing a pointer twice, freeing something that was not returned by an allocation function (a local, or an interior pointer such as p + 1) is undefined behaviour.

items.prompt: After these statements, which description of b is correct?
choices: b is NULL because a was set to NULL
b still points to a valid int that holds 1
b is a dangling pointer: dereferencing it is undefined
b must also be freed, because free(a) only released a's copy
items.explanation: free releases the block, not one particular variable. Every copy of the pointer, including b, now refers to storage whose lifetime ended. Setting a to NULL protects only the variable a, not copies of it, and freeing b would be a double free.

items.prompt: Type exactly what this program prints.
items.explanation: Assigning a struct copies its members, and a pointer member is copied as an address, not as the memory it points to. a.p and b.p refer to the same int, so the write through b.p is visible through a.p. Only one free is needed and the owner must be decided: here buf.

items.prompt: Type exactly what this program prints.
items.explanation: count * sizeof(int) does not fit in size_t. calloc has to supply room for count elements of that size, so it detects the overflow instead of wrapping and fails with NULL (prints 1 on mainstream implementations). With malloc(count * sizeof *p) the product would silently wrap to a small number, so the caller has to test count <= SIZE_MAX / sizeof *p itself.

items.prompt: A constructor function allocates a struct, then allocates two buffers for it, and the second buffer's malloc fails. What must the function do before returning, and how can you structure the code so every error path does this correctly?
items.answer: It must free exactly the resources it has already acquired (the first buffer and the struct), return a failure indicator such as NULL so the caller knows there is nothing to free, and never leave a partially built object visible. A reliable structure is a single cleanup path, for example goto labels in reverse order of acquisition or initializing all pointers to NULL and freeing them at one label because free(NULL) is harmless.

items.prompt: checked_bytes(count, elem_size) should return count * elem_size when both are positive and the product is at most 1000000000, and -1 otherwise (it is meant to guard an allocation size). It returns a small positive number for some huge counts. Fix it.
items.explanation: Checking the product after multiplying is too late: the unsigned multiplication wraps modulo 2^64, so 4611686018427387905 * 4 becomes 4, which passes the limit. Test count against limit / elem_size before multiplying.

items.prompt: Write with_appended(values, n, extra, returnSize): return a NEW heap array that holds the n elements of values followed by extra, and store its length in *returnSize. The caller will free the result. If allocation fails, return NULL and set *returnSize to 0. Do not modify values. (The array argument arrives as a pointer plus its length n.)
items.explanation: Allocate n + 1 elements with the size tied to the element type, check for NULL, copy the n existing elements, append extra, and report the new length. Returning a new allocation transfers ownership to the caller.

items.prompt: After `char dst[4]; strncpy(dst, "abcd", sizeof dst);` which statement is true?
choices: dst holds the characters a, b, c, d and no terminator, so it is not a valid string
dst holds "abc" followed by a terminating zero byte, because strncpy reserves room for it
dst holds "abcd" because strncpy always terminates its result with a zero byte
The call is rejected at run time because the source is longer than the destination allows
items.explanation: strncpy copies at most n characters and writes no terminator when the source has n or more characters. With n equal to sizeof dst, all four bytes are letters. Terminate explicitly (dst[sizeof dst - 1] = '\0') after copying at most sizeof dst - 1, or use snprintf.

items.prompt: What does this program print?
items.explanation: The array holds the five letters and the terminating zero byte, so sizeof s is 6. strlen counts the characters before the terminator: 5.

items.prompt: Which of these code fragments has defined behaviour?
choices: char* s = "abc"; s[0] = 'x';
const char* s = "abc"; ((char*)s)[1] = 'x';
char* s = "abc"; strcpy(s, "xyz");
char s[] = "abc"; s[0] = 'x';
items.explanation: A string literal may be stored in read-only memory and modifying it is undefined behaviour, however the pointer is declared or cast. char s[] = "abc" creates a writable array that is initialized from the literal.

items.prompt: `int n = snprintf(buf, size, "%s", src);` returns the length the full output would have had (n >= 0 here, size > 0). Which test reports that the output was truncated?
choices: n > size
n == size - 1
(size_t)n >= size
buf[size - 1] != '\0'
items.explanation: snprintf writes at most size - 1 characters plus a terminator, so the output fits exactly when n < size. n > size misses the case n == size, where the last character did not fit; n == size - 1 is the exact-fit case; buf[size - 1] is always the terminator after a truncating call.

items.prompt: Type exactly what this program prints.
items.explanation: snprintf stores at most sizeof buf - 1 = 7 characters and a terminator, so buf is "abcdefg". The return value is the length of the untruncated output, 10; since 10 >= 8, the caller can tell it was truncated.

items.prompt: Type exactly what this program prints.
items.explanation: sizeof s is the array size, 6. The initializer sets the first elements and zeroes the rest, so the string ends after "ab": strlen is 2 and s[5] is 0.

items.prompt: Why is `strncpy(dst, src, sizeof dst)` not a safe drop-in replacement for strcpy, and what would you do instead when copying into a fixed-size buffer?
items.answer: strncpy copies at most n characters but writes no terminating zero byte when the source has n or more characters, so dst may not be a valid string and later string functions read past the array. It also pads short copies with zeros, which wastes work. Instead pass the capacity and use snprintf, which always terminates and returns the length it wanted so truncation can be detected, or check the length first and copy with memcpy, or terminate dst[size - 1] explicitly.

items.prompt: last_char_code(s) should return the character code of the last character of s as a nonnegative number, or -1 when s is the empty string. It misbehaves on the empty string. Fix it.
items.explanation: strlen returns size_t, which is unsigned: for the empty string n - 1 wraps to a huge value, so n - 1 >= 0 is always true and the code reads s[n - 1] before the start of the string. Test n > 0 instead.

items.prompt: Write take_prefix(s, n): return a NEW heap-allocated string that holds the first n characters of s, or all of s when it is shorter than n. If n is 0 or negative the result is the empty string. The result must always be properly terminated, and the caller will free it. Return NULL only if allocation fails.
items.explanation: Compute how many characters to take (clamped to 0..strlen(s)), allocate that many plus one byte for the terminator, copy with memcpy and write the terminator explicitly.

items.prompt: After `FILE* f = fopen(path, "r");` returns a non-NULL pointer, a program runs `if (errno != 0) { report_failure(); }`. Why is that test unreliable?
choices: Success does not clear errno, so a nonzero value may be left over from an earlier failure
errno is reset to 0 by every successful library call, so the test can never be true
errno can only be read once per program run, so a second test always sees zero
errno is only meaningful for functions that return a pointer, never for those that return an int
items.explanation: Functions that set errno do so when they fail; a successful call does not promise to clear it, so a stale nonzero value proves nothing. Check the documented failure return value first (NULL for fopen), and only then read errno.

items.prompt: Why do robust callers of strtol set `errno = 0;` immediately before the call?
choices: strtol refuses to start parsing while errno holds a nonzero value from an earlier call
Setting errno to 0 is what makes the call safe to use from several threads at once
It tells strtol to store the position of the first unparsed character in endptr
LONG_MAX can be a real result or an overflow marker, and strtol never clears errno on success
items.explanation: The return value alone cannot separate a range error from a legitimate LONG_MAX. strtol sets errno to ERANGE on overflow but does not reset it on success, so clear it first and test it afterwards.

items.prompt: Which loop processes every line of the open stream f exactly once and then lets you tell end-of-file from a read error?
items.explanation: feof becomes true only after a read has already tried to go past the end, so the first loop processes stale data after the last line. Loop on the return value of the read; afterwards ferror(f) distinguishes a read error from a normal end of file.

items.prompt: What is the weakness of `return -errno;` in this function?
choices: fopen never sets errno on any platform, so the returned value is always 0 here
-errno is not a valid expression, because errno is a macro and cannot be negated
The fprintf call before errno is read may change it, so errno should be saved first
A function must return a positive number to signal an error, so the sign is wrong
items.explanation: Any library call in between, including fprintf, may change errno (even on success). Save it right after the failing call: `int saved = errno;`. (Which functions set errno is partly defined by C and partly by POSIX; fopen setting it is POSIX behaviour.)

items.prompt: Type exactly what this program prints.
items.explanation: strtol converts the leading digits and stops at the first character that cannot be part of the number, setting end to that position ("ab"). Trailing characters are not a range error, so errno stays 0: a robust parser must check *end != '\0' itself.

items.prompt: Type exactly what this program prints.
items.explanation: The number is far larger than any long, so strtol sets errno to ERANGE and returns LONG_MAX. The return value alone would look like a legitimate LONG_MAX; errno (cleared before the call) is what reports the overflow.

items.prompt: A parsing function returns an int and returns 0 whenever the text is not a valid number. What is wrong with this design, and how would you redesign the contract?
items.answer: Returning 0 on failure is ambiguous: the caller cannot tell the valid input "0" from an error, so a failure turns into a plausible result. Redesign it to report success separately: return a status code (or a bool) and deliver the number through an output pointer parameter, and document that the output is left unchanged on failure. Another option is a distinct sentinel that cannot be a valid result, if one exists.

items.prompt: parse_or_default(text, fallback) should return the decimal value of text, or fallback when text has no digits, has any trailing characters after the number, or does not fit in a long long. (text never contains whitespace.) It accepts some invalid inputs. Fix it.
items.explanation: A complete strtoll check has three parts: no digits (end == text), trailing characters (*end != '\0'), and a range error (errno == ERANGE, with errno cleared before the call).

items.prompt: Write digits_value(text): return the value of text, a non-empty string of decimal digits, or -1 on any error. Errors are: the empty string, any character that is not a digit, or a value greater than 1000000000. Detect the last error while accumulating, so that no intermediate result can overflow.
items.explanation: Return -1 for the empty string, test each character, and stop as soon as the value exceeds the limit. Because the value never exceeds 1000000000 before the next step, value * 10 + digit cannot overflow a long long.

items.prompt: Type both numbers this program prints, including their signs.
items.explanation: C99 and later round integer division toward zero, so -7 / 2 is -3 rather than -4. The remainder takes the sign of the dividend, so -7 % 2 is -1.

items.prompt: With uint8_t a = 200 and uint8_t b = 100, what value does s hold after uint8_t s = a + b;?
items.explanation: a + b is computed as an int, 300, and storing it in a uint8_t keeps the value modulo 256, so 300 - 256 = 44. The result is never 300 or negative because uint8_t is unsigned.

items.prompt: Choose the line this program prints.
items.explanation: total / 2 divides two int values, so the division truncates to 3 before the result is converted to double. The .5 is lost, and %.1f prints 3.0.

items.prompt: Explain why assigning int a * int b to a long long can overflow even though the destination is wide enough, and what changes when one operand is converted first.
items.answer: The multiplication is computed in int first, so an overflowing product is already undefined behaviour before it is stored in the long long. Casting one operand to long long, or otherwise converting one operand first, makes the multiplication itself happen in the wider type, so the product fits.

items.prompt: Write count_bits(x): return the number of 1 bits in the binary form of x. x is zero or a positive integer below 2^40.
items.explanation: x & 1 tests the lowest bit and x >>= 1 moves the next bit into that position. The loop stops when no 1 bits remain, so the accumulator holds the count.

items.prompt: Type the three numbers this program prints, in order.
items.explanation: n > 5 is false, so && skips ++checked and big is 0. n > 1 is true, so || skips ++checked and any is 1. checked never changes and stays 0.

items.prompt: A rule accepts a score from 60 to 79 inclusive and rejects everything else. Which condition is correct?
choices: 60 < score && score < 79
60 <= score && score <= 79
score >= 60 || score <= 79 || score < 0
items.explanation: The && form with <= on both sides accepts exactly 60 through 79. Strict comparisons drop both boundaries. The chained form parses as (60 <= score) <= 79 and accepts 0. The || form is true for every score, so it accepts everything.

items.prompt: Pick the number this program prints.
items.explanation: low <= value is 0 because 1 <= 0 is false, and then 0 <= high is 1. The chain prints 1 even though 0 lies outside the range 1 to 5. Write each comparison out and join them with &&.

items.prompt: Why must a bounds check placed before an array read be joined to that read with &&, and why does the read never happen when the check fails?
items.answer: The && operator is short-circuit: when the bounds check is false the whole expression is already false, so the array read is not evaluated. That order keeps an out of bounds index from ever being read.

items.prompt: Write is_leap_year(year): return 1 when year is a leap year in the Gregorian calendar and 0 otherwise. year is between 1 and 9999.
items.explanation: A year is a leap year when it is divisible by 4, except century years, which must also be divisible by 400. && binds tighter than ||, so the parentheses group the 4 and 100 tests before the 400 test is added.

items.prompt: Type both numbers this program prints, in the order they appear.
items.explanation: strlen counts the three letters before the terminator, but sizeof word counts the whole array, including the zero byte, which makes 4.

items.prompt: The string text is valid and terminated. Which loop visits every character exactly once and stops at the terminator?
choices: for (size_t i = 0; i <= strlen(text); i++) { use(text[i]); }
for (size_t i = 1; text[i] != '\0'; i++) { use(text[i]); }
size_t i = 0; while (text[i] != '\0') { use(text[i]); i++; }
for (size_t i = 0; text[i] != '\0' || i < 100; i++) { use(text[i]); }
items.explanation: The while loop starts at index 0, stops when it reads the terminator, and increments once per character. The first loop also visits the terminator, the second skips the first character, and the third reads past the terminator when the string is shorter than 100.

items.prompt: Pick the text this program prints.
items.explanation: C requires the digit characters to be consecutive, so '7' + 1 is '8'. The output is 78.

items.prompt: Explain why a string of 5 letters needs 6 bytes of storage, and what the extra byte holds.
items.answer: The extra byte is the terminating zero byte, '\0'. It marks the end of the string, so functions such as strlen can find the length by stopping there; strlen does not count it, which is why the array needs one more byte than the length.

items.prompt: Type the sum this program prints.
items.explanation: The initializer list sets the first two elements, and the remaining three are zeroed, so the sum is 3 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 4.

items.prompt: A function is declared as long long count_above(const long long* values, size_t n). Which statement about values is correct?
choices: sizeof(values) / sizeof(values[0]) gives n inside the function
values holds its own copy of the caller's array, so writes stay local
values is a pointer, so the callee needs the parameter n to know the length
values is an array of n elements, so sizeof(values) equals n times the element size
items.explanation: An array parameter is adjusted to a pointer to its first element, so sizeof measures the pointer and the length must be passed separately. The const promises that the function does not write through values.

items.prompt: Choose the exact output of this program.
items.explanation: p points at the first element of a, so p[1] = 9 writes a[1]. *(p + 2) reads a[2], which is still 3, so the program prints 9 3.

items.prompt: A dynamic array grows by allocating a larger block and copying. Why must code that holds a pointer to an element re-read it after a push, and what should it keep instead?
items.answer: The growth step can move the whole block to a new address, so the old pointer is stale and using it is undefined behaviour. Keep the index of the element instead and read it again through the array after each push.

items.prompt: A frequency map is built from parallel arrays of words and counts. What must happen the first time a word is seen?
choices: Its existing count must be incremented before any entry exists
The count is set to 0 and the word is ignored until it appears again
A new entry is added with the word as its key and a count of 1
The whole table must be rebuilt from scratch before the count changes
items.explanation: There is no entry to increment yet, so the word must be added as a new entry with count 1. Incrementing a missing entry, or ignoring the word, gives wrong counts.

items.prompt: Type the count this program prints.
items.explanation: strcmp returns 0 when the two strings have the same characters, so the three entries equal to ab are counted. The entries a and b differ.

items.prompt: Explain what goes wrong if a frequency map increments the count for a key it has never stored, and what the program should do first.
items.answer: The lookup finds no entry, so the key is not found, and reading or incrementing a count there is undefined. The program should first add a new entry for the key with a count of 1, or treat the missing count as 0 before adding.

items.prompt: Type the two values printed by this program, in order.
items.explanation: Subtracting two pointers gives the number of elements between them, 3 here, and p + 1 points to the second element, which holds 20.

items.prompt: Which function is safe to call and then dereference the returned pointer?
choices: int *f(void) { int x = 4; return &x; }
int *f(void) { static int x = 4; return &x; }
int *f(void) { int x = 4; int *p = &x; return p + 1; }
int *f(void) { int xs[2] = {1, 2}; return xs; }
items.explanation: A static local has static storage duration and lives for the whole program, so its address stays valid after the call. The other three return an address into, or just past, a local variable whose lifetime has ended when the function returns.

items.prompt: Pick the value this program prints.
items.explanation: calls is a static local, so it keeps its value between calls and is initialized only once. The third call makes it 3.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between an object with automatic storage and one with static storage, and what happens to a pointer to each after the function that made it returns.
items.answer: Automatic storage, such as a local variable, lives on the stack only while its function runs, so a pointer to it dangles after the return and using it is undefined. Static storage lasts for the whole program, so a pointer to a static local stays valid.

items.prompt: Given const int *p and int *const q, which statement is correct?
choices: p can be moved to point at another object, but *p cannot be written through p
q can point elsewhere, but *q can never change
Both p and *p are read-only
Neither p nor *p can ever be changed, so the declaration of q is useless and should be removed
items.explanation: In const int *p the const applies to the int, so p may change while *p may not. In int *const q the const applies to the pointer, so q is fixed while *q may change.

items.prompt: Type both numbers printed on the one line, in order.
items.explanation: a + b is computed as int, 260, so the second value printed is 260. Storing the sum in a uint8_t keeps 260 modulo 256, which is 4.

items.prompt: A function must return a + b for int a and b without overflowing. Which check is valid under C's rules?
choices: if (a + b < a) { return INT_MAX; }
if (b > 0 ? a > INT_MAX - b : a < INT_MIN - b) { return error; }
if (a + b < 0) { return error; }
if (a > INT_MAX - b) { return error; } /* assumes b is never negative */
items.explanation: Check before adding. For positive b the sum overflows exactly when a is above INT_MAX - b, and for zero or negative b it overflows exactly when a is below INT_MIN - b; both subtractions stay in range. The other three tests run after an overflow has already happened or ignore negative b.

items.prompt: Choose the printed result of this program.
items.explanation: Shifting 1 left by 31 sets the top bit of an unsigned 32-bit value, which is defined for unsigned types. Shifting it right by 30 leaves 2. Shifting a signed 1 into the sign bit would be undefined behaviour.

items.prompt: Explain why comparing result with value after computing value + 1 does not detect signed overflow in C, and what a correct check does instead.
items.answer: Signed overflow is undefined behaviour, so once value + 1 has overflowed there is no defined result to compare, and an optimizer may delete the test. A correct check compares value with INT_MAX before the addition and returns early when they are equal.

items.prompt: Write add_or_clamp(a, b): return a + b, except that the result is LLONG_MAX when the true sum is above LLONG_MAX and LLONG_MIN when it is below LLONG_MIN. The function must never overflow.
items.explanation: Each overflow test runs before the addition: a positive b overflows when a exceeds LLONG_MAX - b, and a negative b overflows when a is below LLONG_MIN - b. Both subtractions stay in range, so the function never overflows.

items.prompt: Type the line this program prints.
items.explanation: The #if line is evaluated by the preprocessor before compilation, so only the wide definition reaches the compiler. SCALE * 2 is 6.

items.prompt: main.c declares int transform(int); and calls it. cc -c main.c succeeds. What happens when main.o alone is linked into a program?
choices: The program links and transform returns 0
The compiler reports the missing body during cc -c main.c
The linker reports an undefined reference to transform
The declaration satisfies the linker, so the call runs without a body
items.explanation: A prototype lets the compiler check the call, so cc -c succeeds, but the call needs a definition of transform from some object file or library. main.o alone has none, so the link step fails with an undefined reference to transform.

items.prompt: A header counter.h is included by two .c files. Which line in the header makes linking both objects fail with a multiple definition error?
choices: extern int total;
int total = 0;
int total(void);
static int total = 0; /* one copy per file */
items.explanation: Every object file that includes int total = 0; defines the same external symbol, so the linker sees two definitions. An extern declaration, a function prototype, or a static definition does not produce this error.

items.prompt: util.c defines static int helper(void), and main.c declares int helper(void); and calls it. What happens when both are linked?
choices: The call runs util.c's helper and the link succeeds
The linker reports multiple definitions of helper
The linker keeps main.c's version and ignores util.c's helper
The linker reports an undefined reference to helper
items.explanation: static gives helper internal linkage, so the symbol is invisible to other object files. The declaration in main.c refers to an external helper that nothing defines, so the linker reports an undefined reference.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between compiling and linking a C program, and say which step reports a call to a function whose body is in another file.
items.answer: Compiling turns each translation unit into an object file of machine code that still refers to outside functions by name. Linking combines the object files and resolves each call to its definition; if none exists, the linker reports an undefined reference.
